usage: Used when drawing a conclusion based on visible evidence or a general impression.
example_sentences: It looks like it’s going to rain before we finish the match.
It looks like they have forgotten about the meeting entirely.
It looks like a difficult task, but we can manage it.
It looks like the bus is running late again today.
It looks like everyone is excited about the upcoming holiday.
native_notes: Very common in everyday conversation. Use it when you see something happening and want to describe your immediate deduction.

usage: Used when expressing an intuition or a gut feeling about a future event or someone's intention.
common_mistakes: I have a feel that (wrong noun)
example_sentences: I have a feeling that this project will be a huge success.
I have a feeling that we might have taken the wrong turn.
I have a feeling that the exam is going to be quite challenging.
I have a feeling that she knows more than she is letting on.
I have a feeling that prices will rise by the end of the year.
native_notes: More subjective than 'I think'. It implies that you don't have concrete facts yet, just an instinct.

usage: Used when assessing the probability of an outcome based on experience or trends.
common_mistakes: The chances are that (often 'The' is dropped)
example_sentences: Chances are you will need to book your flight well in advance.
Chances are that the market will stabilize by next month.
Chances are we won't see him at the party tonight.
If you practice daily, chances are your English will improve rapidly.
Chances are the shop is already closed by this hour.
native_notes: A very natural, idiomatic way to express probability. Slightly more casual than 'It is probable that'.

usage: Used to suggest something is highly possible or an expected outcome based on past patterns.
grammar_pattern: I wouldn't be surprised if + subject + past simple (for hypothetical)
common_mistakes: I wouldn't be surprising if (wrong adjective form)
alternatives: It wouldn't come as a shock if
example_sentences: I wouldn't be surprised if he decides to move abroad next year.
I wouldn't be surprised if the company announces layoffs tomorrow.
I wouldn't be surprised if that old car finally breaks down.
I wouldn't be surprised if they win the championship this season.
I wouldn't be surprised if she gets promoted by the end of the term.
native_notes: Use this to soften a prediction. It sounds less aggressive or overly certain than saying 'He will definitely do this'.

usage: Used when providing an estimate when you do not have exact data or information.
alternatives: Off the top of my head
example_sentences: At a guess, I’d say the project will take about three weeks.
At a guess, there were at least five hundred people in the audience.
At a guess, it would cost around two hundred pounds to repair.
At a guess, they’ve lived in that house for over a decade.
At a guess, this is the first time they’ve faced such a challenge.
native_notes: A very useful phrase for IELTS Speaking Part 1 or 2 when the examiner asks for a number or quantity you aren't 100% sure about.

usage: Used to express an opinion or make a guess when you are not 100% sure.
common_mistakes: I guess that he is arrive (wrong tense)
I am guessing (can sound too literal)
example_sentences: I guess we should leave now to avoid the traffic.
I guess that's one way to solve the problem.
Why is she upset? I guess she had a bad day.
I guess it's time to wrap things up.
Do you know the answer? I guess it might be C.
native_notes: Extremely frequent in casual speech. Often used as a filler or a softener when you don't want to sound too assertive.

usage: Used to suggest something is likely true, often involving a bit of intuition or negative suspicion.
common_mistakes: I suspect that he will to go (wrong grammar)
I am suspecting (usually used in simple present)
example_sentences: I suspect that the real reason they left is much more complex.
I suspect this might be a mistake in the original data.
I suspect he is not telling the whole truth.
I suspect that demand for these products will increase.
I suspect there is a misunderstanding regarding the terms.
native_notes: Sounds more analytical than 'I think'. Used when you have gathered some evidence but are not ready to state it as a fact.

uzbek: judayam bo'lishi mumkin, juda haqiqatga yaqin
usage: Used when speculating with a high degree of confidence.
common_mistakes: It may well to be (incorrect verb form)
example_sentences: It might well be the best solution we have available.
It might well be that the market is changing faster than expected.
The reason for the delay might well be the bad weather.
It might well be worth checking the fine print first.
That might well be the case, but we need more evidence.
native_notes: The addition of 'well' significantly increases the degree of probability implied by 'might'.

usage: Used when you have a hunch or a strong feeling about something without being 100% sure.
example_sentences: I suspect that the train will be delayed due to the bad weather.
I suspect that he didn't tell us the whole truth.
I suspect that we are missing a key piece of information.
I suspect that the real reason is much simpler than that.
I suspect that she’s been planning this move for months.
native_notes: Slightly more sophisticated than 'I think' and conveys a nuance of investigating or analyzing.

usage: A common way to talk about probability in a clear, measured way.
grammar_pattern: There's a good chance that + clause
common_mistakes: There have a good chance (incorrect subject)
It has a good chance (idiomatically weaker than 'there is')
alternatives: The odds are in favour of
example_sentences: There's a good chance that this road will be closed for maintenance.
There's a good chance that we can reach a compromise by Friday.
There's a good chance that the economy will recover by next year.
There's a good chance that she will be promoted soon.
There's a good chance that nobody actually knows the answer.
native_notes: More formal and objective than 'chances are', making it excellent for IELTS Writing Task 2.

usage: Used frequently in British English to express a personal opinion or prediction.
common_mistakes: I am reckoning that (usually used in simple present)
example_sentences: I reckon we’ll reach the city by lunchtime.
I reckon the exam will be much harder than the practice test.
I reckon he’s just tired after the long flight.
I reckon there’s a better way to solve this problem.
I reckon it’s time we started our project.
native_notes: Specifically common in UK, Australia, and NZ. Sounds more natural than 'I think' in casual chat.

usage: Used to make a formal, logical prediction about the future or a situation.
example_sentences: In all likelihood, the project will be completed by the end of next month.
In all likelihood, demand for this product will continue to rise.
In all likelihood, there will be some changes to the schedule.
In all likelihood, they will reach an agreement by the end of the day.
In all likelihood, the trend will shift towards digital solutions.
native_notes: Excellent for IELTS Writing Task 2 to show high level of command in logical progression.

usage: Used to express an opinion or an assumption when you are not 100% certain.
example_sentences: I suppose we should start heading to the station now.
I suppose that is one way to interpret the data.
Well, I suppose it’s possible, but it seems unlikely.
I suppose you're right, we need more time to prepare.
I suppose there might be a better way to handle this.
native_notes: Often used to signal reluctance or mild agreement. Saying 'I suppose so' often implies you are not fully convinced.

usage: Used to express a strong possibility about a future or current situation.
grammar_pattern: It could well be that + clause / [Subject] could well be [adjective/noun]
example_sentences: It could well be that the market will crash by the end of the year.
That could well be the reason why they chose to relocate.
The reason for the delay could well be technical failure.
It could well be that we need to rethink our entire strategy.
His reaction could well be a sign that he is hiding something.
native_notes: The word 'well' adds a layer of confidence to the speculation, moving it from 'maybe' to 'very possible'.

usage: Used in academic or professional settings to speculate about the outcome of an event.
grammar_pattern: There is a fair chance that + clause
example_sentences: There is a fair chance that the new policy will improve productivity.
I think there is a fair chance we can meet the deadline.
There is a fair chance that the candidate will accept the job offer.
Given the current trends, there is a fair chance the prices will rise.
There is a fair chance that they might change their minds at the last minute.
native_notes: Native speakers use 'fair' to mean 'good' or 'significant'. It is more sophisticated than saying 'maybe'.

usage: Used when evaluating the probability of a future event occurring.
grammar_pattern: There is a good chance (that) + clause
common_mistakes: There is a big chance (less natural)
It has a good chance (not standard idiomatic usage)
example_sentences: There is a good chance that the event will be postponed.
There is a good chance you will get the job if you prepare well.
There is a good chance of snow by the weekend.
There is a good chance that technology will solve these issues soon.
There is a good chance we can finish the report by tonight.
native_notes: Sounds much more natural and idiomatic than 'it is probable'.

usage: Used when basing an opinion on specific information or evidence available at the time.
common_mistakes: Judging from the facts, ... (slightly different nuance, but acceptable)
example_sentences: Judging by the dark clouds, we are in for a storm.
Judging by the attendance, the campaign has been a huge success.
Judging by his recent performance, he is ready for a promotion.
Judging by the statistics, this trend will continue.
Judging by the lack of response, they are not interested.
collocations: judging by the look of it
native_notes: Use this to add analytical weight to your IELTS Speaking or Writing answers.

usage: Used to suggest a possibility without being certain.
example_sentences: There's a chance that the flight will be delayed due to the storm.
There's a chance that I will finish my essay by Friday.
Do you think there's a chance that they will change the schedule?
There's a slim chance that the team will win, but we remain hopeful.
There's a good chance that this technology will revolutionise the industry.
native_notes: Adding 'good' or 'slim' before 'chance' helps specify how likely you think the event is.

usage: Used in academic or business contexts when drawing a logical conclusion from known data.
grammar_pattern: It is fair to assume that + clause
common_mistakes: It is fair for assume (incorrect preposition)
example_sentences: Given the recent decline in sales, it is fair to assume that the strategy failed.
It is fair to assume that the population will continue to age in the coming decades.
It is fair to assume that most students have access to the internet.
Based on these results, it is fair to assume that the hypothesis is correct.
It is fair to assume that the new regulations will be enforced by next month.
native_notes: Perfect for IELTS Writing Task 2 when interpreting a graph or explaining an argument.

uzbek: Hammasini hisobga olganda / hamma narsani inobatga olgan holda
usage: Used when summarizing thoughts and making an informed speculation after considering all available facts.
common_mistakes: Take everything into account (wrong participle form)
alternatives: When you weigh up the evidence
example_sentences: Taking everything into account, it seems likely that the market will stabilise by year-end.
Taking everything into account, I would say that the policy has been a moderate success.
Taking everything into account, the company is in a strong position for growth.
Taking everything into account, it is probably better to wait for more information.
Taking everything into account, the decision to relocate appears to be the right one.
native_notes: Perfect for IELTS Writing Task 2 or Speaking Part 3 to show you have evaluated multiple sides of an argument.

expression: There is a strong possibility that
usage: Used in academic or professional settings to speculate with high confidence.
grammar_pattern: There is a strong possibility that + clause
common_mistakes: It is a strong possibility that
There is a strong possibility of to
example_sentences: There is a strong possibility that government policy will shift next year.
There is a strong possibility that current trends will continue into the next decade.
There is a strong possibility that the research will yield significant results.
There is a strong possibility that international trade will face disruptions.
There is a strong possibility that the candidate will accept the position.
native_notes: Ideal for IELTS Writing Task 2 or professional presentations where you want to sound objective.

usage: Used to express that something is likely to happen or be true based on probability.
common_mistakes: There have a good chance (wrong verb)
example_sentences: There's a good chance we will finish the project before Friday.
There's a good chance the traffic will be heavy at this hour.
There's a good chance that interest rates will rise next quarter.
If you study hard, there's a good chance you'll pass the exam.
There's a good chance they have already left for the airport.
native_notes: More natural than 'it is probable' in conversation.

usage: Used when speculating cautiously but with a degree of confidence or acknowledgement of possibility.
grammar_pattern: It might well be that + clause
common_mistakes: It may well to be (incorrect infinitive)
example_sentences: It might well be that the market is already oversaturated.
It might well be that he decided to resign for personal reasons.
It might well be that technology will solve this crisis eventually.
It might well be that the original plan was too ambitious.
It might well be that they are waiting for a better offer.
native_notes: The 'well' adds a professional, sophisticated touch to the speculation.
